strengths: Novel and rigorously formalized notion of group fairness in optimal transport (F-fair couplings) that is more modular than prior work

Solid theoretical contributions including finite-sample complexity bounds for penalized OT (Theorem 4.2) showing fairness penalty does not degrade O(1/√n) rate, and fairness generalization bounds for cost learning (Theorem 4.4)
Elegant algorithmic framework: Proposition 3.3 shows fair OT solution has Sinkhorn form, enabling FairSinkhorn algorithm with guaranteed convergence
Two complementary practical approaches (penalized OT and cost learning) with clear trade-offs: convexity vs. reusability and interpretability
Clear, well-motivated presentation with compelling real-world examples (dating apps, school admissions, kidney allocation) and effective illustrations
Comprehensive implementation details supporting reproducibility; promise to release code upon publication
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only synthetic data (Gaussians, circles) despite multiple real-world motivating applications; no empirical validation of theoretical sample complexity rates; no comparison with fairness-aware matching baselines

Loose theoretical bounds: Theorem 4.4's exp(5R_Θε^{-1})/√n dependence is exponential in ε^{-1}; with ε=2 this could be exp(2.5R_Θ) which may be very large depending on cost scale; practical implications not discussed

Asymmetric theoretical coverage: Theorem 4.2 provides sample complexity for penalized OT but no generalization bound for cost learning provided (acknowledged as future work), weakening the cost learning contribution

Fairness target specification largely unaddressed in practice: no guidance on how to determine appropriate F values; no analysis of sensitivity to misspecified F; no discussion of whether F itself could encode discrimination or historical biases

Missing practical guidance on key hyperparameters: choice of fairness penalty λ, tolerance ρ, discrepancy measure D, and baseline cost in cost learning left without systematic guidance or sensitivity analysis
Non-convex bilevel optimization in cost learning acknowledged to risk local minima but not empirically analyzed; computational complexity with respect to number of groups not characterized
Limited ablation studies: no sensitivity analysis for fairness target F, no study of effect of entropic regularization ε on fairness-utility trade-off, no analysis of failure modes
Assumption 4.1 (infinite differentiability of cost) could exclude some natural costs; brief discussion of necessity would strengthen presentation

strengths: Addresses important and socially relevant problem of fairness in algorithmic matching with compelling real-world applications
Technically sound mathematical framework with clear formalization of F-fair couplings and proper derivation of solution structure
Offers multiple solution approaches with different computational-reusability tradeoffs (exact, penalized, cost-learning)
Novel sample complexity result (Theorem 4.2) showing fairness penalties do not worsen statistical efficiency
Generalization bounds for learned costs on test data (Theorem 4.4) enable cost reuse
weaknesses: Critical gap: Paper never addresses how practitioners should choose the fairness target matrix F, which is fundamental to the approach and undermines practical applicability
Insufficient experimental validation: Only synthetic datasets with tiny sample sizes (20 samples per group); no real-world experiments, no comparison to alternative methods, no ablation studies
Theorem 4.4 bound contains exp(5R_Θ ε⁻¹) term that becomes vacuous for practical entropic regularization strengths, severely limiting utility despite acknowledgment
Fairness definition not justified: No explanation for why marginal group constraints constitute fairness or discussion of when this notion is appropriate versus individual fairness
Non-convex bilevel optimization for cost learning lacks convergence analysis, convergence guarantees, or empirical validation of convergence behavior
Limited novelty: Core contribution combines existing OT techniques with straightforward linear constraints; sample complexity proof heavily adapts Rigollet & Stromme [58] with minor modifications
Missing practical guidance: How to select fairness penalty λ, interaction between entropy regularization ε and fairness, computational complexity, or when each approach is preferred

Incomplete fairness conceptualization: No engagement with fairness literature concerns (disparate impact, uncertainty), and ethical implications (e.g., dating app homogamy) presented without discussion

strengths: Novel problem formulation introducing group fairness directly to optimal transport with clear motivation through real-world matching applications
Solid theoretical contributions including sample complexity bound for penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2) with O(1/√n) rate generalizable to arbitrary convex penalties
Comprehensive framework with three complementary approaches: exact FairSinkhorn algorithm with elegant dual form (Prop 3.3), convex penalized formulation, and non-convex cost learning
Practical algorithmic contributions demonstrated with 3-4 orders of magnitude speedup for reusable costs (Figure 7) enabling efficient matching of new samples
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, effective Pareto front visualizations, and rigorous proofs that appear technically sound
Addresses an important gap in fairness literature by studying group fairness in matching problems rather than supervised/unsupervised learning
weaknesses: Insufficient experimental validation: Only synthetic datasets (Gaussian, concentric circles) with no real-world case studies despite motivating examples of college admissions, kidney allocation, and dating platforms - critical limitation for ICML

Cost learning theory incomplete: provides only deviation bound (Theorem 4.4) on fairness, not generalization bound on learned cost parameters; exponential dependence exp(5R_Θε^{-1})/√n becomes loose for small ε when accurate OT is needed

Limited practical guidance on choosing fairness targets F: paper requires 'central planner' specification but provides no methodology; no discussion of sensitivity, infeasibility, or intersectional fairness
Missing baseline comparisons: no comparison with fairness-aware matching or constrained OT methods from existing literature, making it unclear if proposed approach is preferable
Bilevel cost learning underperforms compared to penalized OT in experiments (Figures 3, 5) and lacks convergence rate analysis despite being non-convex; unclear when to prefer this approach
Restricted fairness definition captures only group-level matching probabilities; does not address individual-level fairness or intersectional concerns; no discussion of unintended consequences
Limited algorithmic analysis: FairSinkhorn convergence deferred, no sensitivity analysis for entropy regularization ε, no systematic hyperparameter selection, reproducibility relies on promised code

strengths: Novel fairness notion for optimal transport: Fairness targets are intuitive, flexible, and naturally encode real-world constraints (homogamy reduction, quotas, diversity) that are well-motivated through compelling applications.

Solid theoretical contributions: Novel sample complexity bound for penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2) matching O(n^{-1/2}) rate, and uniform fairness deviation bounds over learned cost families (Theorem 4.4); proofs appear technically sound.

Multiple complementary solution approaches: FairSinkhorn (exact fairness, convex), penalized OT (fine-grained control, convex), and cost learning (reusable, interpretable) provide a useful menu with different trade-offs.
Well-motivated problem formulation with clear distinction from prior work: Difference from individual fairness approaches and problem-specific fairness constraints is clearly articulated.

Reasonable experimental validation: Synthetic experiments clearly demonstrate fairness-cost trade-offs, semi-synthetic dating app experiment shows real-world applicability, and validation of learned cost reusability and generalization.
Clear presentation: Well-written with good motivation, illustrative figures (especially Figure 1), and clear problem formulation accessible to ICML audience.
weaknesses: Exponential dependencies severely limit practical utility of theoretical bounds: Theorem 4.2 and 4.4 have exponential scaling in ε and ε^{-1} respectively. Authors acknowledge these are 'unavoidable in worst case' but provide no mitigation. For small ε (needed for tight fairness control), bounds become vacuous in practice.

Significant gap between theory and experiments: Sample complexity bounds only provide asymptotic rates with hidden constants; experiments use small samples (e.g., 250/25) contradicting the large sample sizes suggested by bounds. No empirical validation of when bounds are tight or useful.

Cost learning analysis incomplete: Bilevel optimization is non-convex with no convergence guarantees. Theorem 4.4 bounds deviation from population but not actual fairness improvement. No analysis of how often algorithm gets stuck in poor local minima.

Limited algorithmic novelty: FairSinkhorn is straightforward extension adding one projection step; penalized approach uses standard conditional gradient; cost learning uses off-the-shelf bilevel optimization. While technically sound, techniques are relatively incremental.

Fairness target specification inadequately addressed: No guidance on how practitioners should set fairness targets in practice. Paper appropriately notes this is a 'political, philosophical and ethical decision' but provides no methodology. No sensitivity analysis on how results change with different targets.

Experimental scope is limited: Only 2 groups in synthetic experiments; low-dimensional data; dating app uses 'simulated compatibility matrix' from sexual orientation rather than actual preferences; no comparison with other fairness-aware matching methods; missing ablation studies.
Computational complexity analysis missing: No asymptotic complexity analysis; cost learning computational cost not thoroughly discussed; scalability to large problems unclear.
Individual fairness completely unaddressed: Limitation acknowledged but no discussion of conflicts between group and individual fairness, which may be important for practical applications.

Deterministic matching analysis underdeveloped: Remark 3.3 and Figure 7b briefly address conversion from probabilistic to deterministic plans, but analysis is incomplete. Should characterize sample sizes needed to maintain fairness.
Limited exploration of natural extensions: Range-based constraints (Remark 4.1) not experimentally explored; weighted fairness and soft constraints not discussed despite practical relevance.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing fairness in matching algorithms with concrete applications
Mathematically sound framework with rigorous formulation and existence/uniqueness results (Prop 3.2)
Multiple complementary methodological approaches (exact constraints, penalization, cost learning) offering different trade-offs
Novel theoretical contributions including sample complexity bounds (Theorem 4.2) and fairness deviation bounds (Theorem 4.4) for statistical OT
Clear presentation with good intuitive examples and informative figures
Principled extension of Sinkhorn algorithm capturing fairness constraints elegantly (Prop 3.3)
weaknesses: Critical practical gap: No guidance on how practitioners should specify fairness targets F, despite acknowledging this as a central design choice
Weak experimental validation: Relies heavily on synthetic Gaussian/circular data; dating app experiment uses semi-synthetic compatibility with unclear realism
Missing baselines: No comparison to other fairness-aware matching algorithms; only compares variants of the proposed method
Restrictive theoretical bounds: Exponential dependence on λ and ε in Theorems 4.2-4.4 makes bounds potentially vacuous for practical problem sizes; claims about 'reasonable values' are unprincipled
Limited novelty of fairness notion: Straightforward adaptation of group fairness to OT; extensions to range-based constraints mentioned but underdeveloped
Insufficient analysis of fairness-cost trade-offs: No characterization of when fairness is expensive, fundamental limits, or decision rules for selecting trade-off points
No convergence rate analysis for FairSinkhorn; unclear how convergence scales with fairness constraints
Cost learning is non-convex bilevel optimization but lacks discussion of local minima, initialization sensitivity, or convergence guarantees
Missing ablations: No sensitivity analysis to fairness target misspecification, imbalanced groups, or different fairness metrics
Limited treatment of converting probabilistic to deterministic plans; important discussion relegated to appendix

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: The notion of fairness targets F is genuinely new for optimal transport literature, mapping naturally to real-world regulatory rules (four-fifths rule, quotas, diversity targets)

Strong technical contributions across three complementary approaches: (1) FairSinkhorn with elegant dual formulation enabling efficient computation, (2) penalized OT with novel sample complexity bound O(n^{-1/2}) matching standard entropic OT, (3) cost learning with generalization bounds for reuse on unseen data

Rigorous and complete mathematical framework: Sound assumptions clearly stated, well-structured proofs with appropriate techniques (sandwich argument in Theorem 4.2, extension of Rigollet & Stromme for Theorem 4.4), and proper establishment of existence/uniqueness of solutions

Clear algorithmic contributions with well-articulated trade-offs: The paper effectively compares when to use exact fairness (FairSinkhorn), fine-grained fairness-cost control (penalized OT), or reusable solutions (cost learning)

Comprehensive presentation: Clear writing, compelling real-world motivation (school segregation, dating homogamy, kidney allocation), thorough related work positioning the contribution, effective figures, and complete appendices with full proofs and implementation details

Reasonable experimental validation: Effective progression from synthetic to semi-realistic datasets, demonstrations of key properties including fairness generalization and learned cost reusability, multiple cost parametrizations tested (Mahalanobis, neural networks)
weaknesses: Significant exponential dependence in theoretical bounds limits practical applicability: Both Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 have exponential terms (exp(R_Θ/ε), exp(λK_sK_w/ε)) that become prohibitive for small ε or many groups. While inherited from prior work, this severely constrains practical utility of the guarantees

Limited scope of fairness notion restricted to group fairness: Does not address individual fairness (similar individuals receiving similar outcomes), and experiments only demonstrate binary sensitive attributes. No analysis of how fairness targets affect downstream individual outcomes—a significant practical gap

Experimental limitations reduce confidence in practical performance: Limited scale (<1000 samples), no computational complexity analysis or timing comparisons between methods, Circles dataset is somewhat artificial, dating app uses simulated compatibility assumptions, no comparison to alternative fairness-constrained matching baselines

Significant gap between theory and practice: Sample complexity bounds are asymptotic with hidden constants, no finite-sample guidelines for practitioners, limited guidance on practical selection of λ, ε, and fairness target F. Theorem 4.4's exponential dependence on ε implies poor generalization for reasonable regularization levels

Design choices not well-justified: Use of L² norm for fairness loss (Eq. 4) not motivated, choice of D(·,·) penalty not analyzed for sensitivity, experimental hyperparameter grids appear arbitrary (e.g., logspace(0,4,80))

Limited discussion of practical deployment: Impact statement appropriately defers fairness target design to stakeholders but offers minimal guidance. No discussion of monitoring deployed systems, detecting dataset shift, or feedback loops. Fairness target must be valid coupling—verification constraint not highlighted
